chapters.relation: The editors answer Asimov's and Posner's dismissals of 1984 as obsolete by pointing to the Iraq War's 935 false statements, Snowden's NSA surveillance disclosures, weaponized social media, and Kellyanne Conway's 'alternative facts' as evidence that we may live in Orwell's world in 2018. They argue technology is not the antidote to Orwellian concerns, despite Apple's famous '1984 won't be like Nineteen Eighty-Four' ad, since telescreen-like smartphones and the Party's history-rewriting bureaucracy are both forms of 'political technology'. The real antidote is philosophy, which trains us to examine assumptions and resist bad arguments, as Winston feared when he thought any Party intellectual could overthrow him in debate.

chapters.file: ch11 - 1. Revolutionary from the Waist Down.md
chapters.relation: Storrie and Martin use Foucault's critique of the repressive hypothesis to argue that Winston is wrong to think sex is naturally subversive and the Party merely represses it. Power over sexuality is productive: the Soviet sexual revolution, Ceausescu's Decree 770 and its 'Decree Generation', Pornosec's pornography for pacifying proles, and tacitly tolerated prostitution all channel erotic energy into state power rather than simply forbid it. Reading O'Brien's torture of Winston as a sustained scene of rape and castration (following Cass Sunstein), they conclude that only understanding power's productive use of sex, as Julia does, makes effective resistance possible; it is Winston who turns out to be merely 'a revolutionary from the waist down'.

Di Nucci compares the Party's mandatory morning Physical Jerks to the modern middle-class ritual of pre-work exercise, asking who needs an oppressor when we oppress ourselves. He argues exercise carries a hidden political price: the time, energy, and solitude it consumes (Orwell shows exercise making it harder for Winston to think and remember) leave citizens too exhausted for the political engagement Aristotle considered necessary to the good life. Like Juvenal's bread and circuses, now 'panem et iphones', and like private schooling, fitness culture also deepens class inequality because working-class people lack the time and energy to access it.

chapters.file: ch13 - 3. Why Don’t the Proles Just Take Over.md
chapters.relation: Littmann asks why Oceania's proles, 85 percent of the population who could 'blow the Party to pieces tomorrow morning', never revolt, answering with Winston's diagnosis: until they become conscious they will never rebel. The Party keeps them unconscious through its media monopoly, crimestop, doublethink, reality control, perpetual war hysteria, and a nationalist identity that cuts them off from the international proletariat. He maps each mechanism onto the modern US, where six corporations control about 90 percent of media, citizens tailor their own reality bubbles, opponents are assumed to argue in bad faith, and partisan 'nationalisms' block common cause, arguing that American political conflict is mostly over facts rather than values.

Nash argues 1984 has been misread as a critique of state power alone; through Newspeak's silencing of thought (in the tradition Austin, MacKinnon, and Langton developed) it shows how any concentration of power oppresses via control of words, data, and information. Drawing on Goldstein's manual's debt to James Burnham's managerial revolution and Sheldon Wolin's 'inverted totalitarianism', she reads the non-centralized Oceania as a warning about non-state enemies: corporations, think tanks running the 'Tobacco Strategy', and global institutions peddling misleading poverty statistics. Popper, Arendt, and Berlin exemplify the state-focused liberalism she thinks blinded us to these horizontal threats, while the Newspeak appendix's past tense shows Orwell expected totalitarianism to be beatable through evidence and democracy.

chapters.file: ch15 - 5. Ministry of Truth Handbook Excerpt on the Strategic Use of Fallacious Reasoning for Thoughtcrime Prevention.md
chapters.relation: Rard's satirical Party handbook explains how to keep a population from thinking: keep the proles too poor and exhausted to reason, and deploy fallacies strategically, from ad hominem goat-caricatures of Goldstein at the Two Minutes Hate and straw man versions of his arguments, to destroying contrary evidence, appealing to fear of the old capitalist world, and Room 101's appeal to force, so false beliefs can be manufactured as easily as true ones. It presents Plato's noble lie as the Ministry's founding inspiration, calling the reader's mission 'a continuation of Plato's dream'. It also cites Aristotle's view that emotion must be disciplined for reason to work, which the Party inverts by deliberately triggering fear and hatred to disable rational thought.

Botello-Samson and Mobley extend Fromm's point that 1984 indicts authoritarian power in general by reading Oceania alongside neoliberalism, which grew out of Locke's liberalism of natural rights and limited government yet demands activist state power to create the conditions for markets. Doublethink reappears as 'accountable independence' in administrative law (Chevron deference, and Garcetti v. Ceballos stripping whistleblower protection) and as Washington Consensus food policy, in which developing nations were pushed off agricultural self-sufficiency while the US kept its own subsidies. Both Ingsoc and neoliberal governance reduce everything to economic elements and use Newspeak-like buzzwords such as 'stakeholder' and 'customer-driven government' to hide the contradiction between democratic rhetoric and rule by experts and elites.

chapters.file: ch18 - 7. Big Brother, We’re Watching You!.md
chapters.relation: Tännsjö argues mass surveillance is here to stay, and since absolute privacy is technically impossible while targeted surveillance only stigmatizes the dissidents who most need protection, we should embrace reciprocal mass surveillance: radical transparency in which citizens can 'watch Big Brother back', secret-service records are opened, and whistleblowers like Snowden and Manning are honored as heroes. On the way he dismantles the standard defenses of privacy, including the honor-based right to control one's image, moral rights (following Thomson's denial of a distinct right to privacy), and dignity-based autonomy arguments, while conceding through Nagel and Rachels what would be lost if inner thoughts became readable. Winston's opening wish to see Big Brother as Big Brother sees him becomes the chapter's model of an open surveillance society.

Koï asks whether biomedical enhancement could make humans resistant to the totalitarian subjugation shown in 1984, where the Party keeps proles too poor and distracted to think and dims Outer Party minds with Newspeak, erased history, and propaganda. Testing Persson and Savulescu's program of enhancing intelligence and moral empathy, she finds intelligence enhancement an educated gamble, since the gifted are also the most likely to embrace extremism and to start totalitarian movements, and empathy politically selective: Nazis directed it only at the in-group and even invoked it to justify the 'euthanasia' murders, while Party propaganda exploits citizens' empathy for horror stories of pre-revolution child labor. Her conclusion is that whatever capacity we enhance, the oligarchy could turn it to its own use: none of us will ever be immune to the love of Big Brother.

Buchanan argues the Party 'sleep-hacks' its citizens because sleep is an active state of thought, a lineage he traces from Aristotle's theory of dreaming through Freud's Interpretation of Dreams, and is therefore a site of potential resistance that must be colonized. Between the Physical Jerks, telescreen trumpet-calls, a Thought Police able to inspect anyone 'asleep or awake' without warning, and O'Brien's manipulation of Winston's sleep schedule during torture, Winston is trapped in 'Newsleep', a derealized blur of dream and reality that makes doublethink the only available way of thinking. He extends the diagnosis to our own 24/7 economy of phones and Trump's all-hours tweets, concluding that Orwell's warning is that we must guard our sleep.

Sandefur argues that what makes totalitarianism unique is its demand that subjects love their ruler, and that this project is doomed because love is selective, unequal, internal, and inalienable, invoking Aristotle's critique of Plato's community of wives and children, Machiavelli on whether rulers should be loved or feared, and Arendt on conscience as internal dialogue and totalitarianism as total rule. Winston and Julia's sex is a political act asserting the individual against the collective, while the Two Minutes Hate channels repressed erotic energy into sanctioned ecstasy directed at Big Brother, as at Khomeini's funeral. What finally breaks Winston in Room 101 is not torture as such but his surrender of Julia, the one thing that was truly his, which collapses the distinction between love and rape.

chapters.file: ch22 - 11. When Cruelty Is Not Enough.md
chapters.relation: Conway argues the real horror of 1984 is not the torture chamber but O'Brien's worldmaking: he cultivated Winston and Julia's affair from lust into a hopeful little home precisely so that destroying it, and hope itself, the Party's true enemy, would be total. Against Rorty's influential reading of O'Brien as a torturer who breaks Winston for pleasure, Conway adds two amendments: Arendt's thoughtless technocrat, with O'Brien as an Eichmann figure whose Party affirms his competence and insulates him from rebuke, and Horkheimer and Adorno's warning that technical rationality has become a secular religion whose 'priests of power' sanctify cruelty. The result is a portrait of a warm-blooded, situationally sympathetic sadist who genuinely excels at building the selves and worlds he is then charged to dismantle.

chapters.file: ch23 - 12. No Crack in the Wall.md
chapters.relation: Silberbusch defends 1984's bleakness with Adorno, for whom 'only exaggeration is true' and unreduced awareness of the worst torture is the first step toward resistance, so that the dystopia negatively preserves the utopia it forbids. She then finds cracks in the wall: Julia's spontaneous 'I love you', the ring-doves and bluebells of the Golden Country, and the 'mute protest in your bones' are the unassimilable other that the Party's megalomaniac calculating rationality, its identity thinking taken to totality, cannot control. Against O'Brien's claim that 'we create human nature', she cites Primo Levi's Muselmänner to argue that humanity survived even Auschwitz, so Big Brother has not truly won.

chapters.file: ch24 - 13. Hangings, Shootings, and Other Funny Stuff in 1984.md
chapters.relation: Hietalahti combines Kierkegaard's thesis that the comic lies in contradiction, Plato's warning that laughter is malicious and must be chained by law, and Bergson's account of laughter as social punishment to explain Oceania's humor: the cinema audience laughs at refugees being machine-gunned, citizens clamor for public hangings, and the barroom joke about living in treetops humiliates the old man, because shared fear and hatred set the norms of what counts as funny. Doublethink explains why slogans like 'War is peace' provoke no laughter in Oceania, and the Ministry of Truth's amusement industry shows the Party deliberately weaponizes fun. The upshot is reflexive: Orwell indicts our own unexamined sense of humor, including the slogan that everything may be ridiculed, not merely Oceania's.

holes.name: Informal Fallacies (ad hominem, straw man, appeal to fear)
holes.what: Standard errors in reasoning, such as ad hominem, straw man, suppressed evidence, and appeals to fear or force, that persuade regardless of the truth of the conclusion.
holes.why: Chapter 15 is structured as a Party handbook teaching the strategic deployment of these exact fallacies to manufacture false beliefs and prevent thoughtcrime.

holes.name: Neoliberalism
holes.what: The doctrine that human well-being is best advanced by liberating entrepreneurial freedoms within strong private property rights, free markets, and free trade, remaking the state on the model of the firm.
holes.why: Chapter 16 argues that 1984's Doublethink and arbitrary bureaucratic power map onto neoliberal governance, from Chevron deference and whistleblower erosion to the Washington Consensus.

holes.name: The Right to Privacy
holes.what: The alleged moral right to control access to information about oneself, one's body, and one's personal space, defended via honor, self-ownership, or dignity.
holes.why: Chapter 18's entire assessment of mass surveillance turns on whether privacy is a right, an honor claim, or a dignity claim, and whether any of these can survive ubiquitous observation.

holes.name: Philosophy of Sleep
holes.what: The view that sleep and dreaming are active modes of thinking in which the mind continues its own work rather than shutting off.
holes.why: Chapter 20 argues the Party sleep-hacks Winston because sleep is a site of independent thought, and that our 24/7 devices impose a 'Newsleep' that erodes the reality-fantasy border.

holes.name: The Nonidentical (identity thinking)
holes.what: Adorno's concept of the unique, ungraspable other that escapes conceptual subsumption, which 'identity thinking' homogenizes; totalitarianism is identity thinking gone mad.
holes.why: Chapter 23 reads Julia's love, the ring-doves, and the body's mute protest as the nonidentical persisting inside Oceania's total identity thinking.

holes.name: Dialectic of Enlightenment (domination of nature)
holes.what: Adorno and Horkheimer's thesis that enlightened reason's drive to subjugate nature within and without turns into instrumental domination, of which totalitarianism is the extreme consequence.
holes.why: Chapter 23 uses this frame to read the Party's megalomaniac calculating rationality and its war on emotion, spontaneity, and nature as enlightenment's self-betrayal.
